paper.abstract:
Abstract Test-time adaptation (TTA) adapts pretrained models to distribution shifts encountered during deployment. However, most existing methods rely primarily on the weight representations of the final layer or signals derived from the model’s output probability distribution. In this work, we study hidden trajectories : the ordered sequence of intermediate representations produced across a deep neural network. We observe that clean and corrupted trajectories become more separable as corruption severity increases. Based on this observation, we introduce Drift-TTA , which adds zero-initialized low-rank adapters to a frozen backbone and trains them to align corrupted hidden trajectories with those from cleaner inputs. The proposed approach supports two variants: a source-dependent version trained with clean targets, and a source-free setting that learns from corrupted images at different severities. Building on these two variants, we further develop an online TTA approach that freezes the backbone and adapters while updating a scalar gate to control adaptation strength. We further cast trajectory alignment as MAP inference under a Gaussian observation model and derive a KL-based transfer bound characterizing
test-time trajectory misalignment in terms of offline residual error, residual dimensionality, and distribution shift between offline and test corruptions. We evaluate Drift-TTA on CIFAR-10-C, CIFAR-100-C, and ImageNet-C using supervised ViTs and CLIP models.
On CIFAR-100-C at severity 5, our source-free online approach improves accuracy over no TTA by 13.3 percentage points with ViT-B/16 and 11.6 percentage points with CLIP ViT-B/16, reaching 74.9% and 47.4%, respectively.
Under the same setting, prior TTA baselines yield ECEs of 18.00% for ViT and 14.70% for CLIP, while our approach reduces them to 9.53% and 5.77%, respectively.
These results demonstrate that hidden trajectory alignment provides an effective signal for both offline correction and lightweight online test-time adaptation.

sections.heading: 1  Introduction
sections.text: Test time adaptation (TTA) adapts a pretrained model to unlabeled test data during deployment, when corruptions such as sensor noise, weather, blur, and compression artifacts shift inputs away from the clean source distribution ( Hendrycks and Dietterich, 2019 ) . Many recent methods guide adaptation using prediction-derived objectives, learned update mechanisms, or auxiliary self-supervised signals ( Liang et al., 2025 ; Xiao and Snoek, 2024 ) . Some minimize entropy or use related confidence and energy objectives to update a small set of model parameters, including the affine parameters of batch normalization layers ( Wang et al., 2021 ; Choi et al., 2025 ) , while others adapt representations or features directly ( Murphy et al., 2026 ; Cho et al., 2025 ) . These studies demonstrate the potential of TTA to recover much of the accuracy lost on standard corruption benchmarks, often with modest computation and without source labels during test time. Entropy minimization is the primary approach in TTA, with several methods extending it through related confidence- and energy-based objectives ( Deng et al., 2025 ; Lei et al., 2025 ) . However, these objectives encourage the model to produce more confident predictions, but do not directly optimize whether those predictions are correct. As a result, an incorrect prediction can become more confident without necessarily being corrected. Furthermore, intermediate features remain comparatively underexplored in TTA, both in how they change as corruption severity increases and in whether they can provide a complementary signal for adaptation. To examine this, we look beyond the final output or a single representation and follow how features evolve through the network. Chain-of-Embedding ( Wang et al., 2025a ) provides a framework for this by representing a forward pass as a trajectory of hidden states whose geometry can differ across outcomes. We extend this view to vision under corruption and examine whether clean and corrupted inputs trace distinguishable trajectories through a ViT or CLIP image tower. Across all models we test, features derived from the hidden trajectory separate clean and corrupted inputs more clearly as corruption severity increases. This observation motivates Drift-TTA , which adds zero-initialized low-rank adapters ( Hu et al., 2022 ) to a frozen backbone and trains them so that corrupted inputs produce hidden trajectories closer to those of their clean counterparts. Figure 1 summarizes this intuition. Corruption progressively displaces the hidden trajectory as severity increases, while Drift-TTA learns a correction in the opposite direction and shifts the resulting trajectory features back toward the clean distribution. Figure 1: Corruption progressively shifts hidden trajectories, while Drift-TTA moves them back toward clean. (a) Schematic of severity-dependent trajectory drift and the correction learned by Drift-TTA. (b) Distributions of the trajectory magnitude and angle features for clean and corrupted inputs at severities 1–5, before and after applying Drift-TTA. Each column compares clean inputs with one corruption severity. Without adaptation, the corrupted distributions move farther from clean as severity increases. With Drift-TTA, they shift back toward the clean distribution. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • We introduce hidden trajectories as a vision-domain extension of the chain-of-embeddings framework previously studied in large language models: A hidden trajectory captures the ordered sequence of mean-pooled representations across backbone layers, and we show that trajectory-derived features increasingly separate clean from corrupted inputs as corruption severity grows across all tested vision models. • We introduce hidden-trajectory alignment as a deployment-efficient mechanism for corruption correction: Drift-TTA instantiates this idea by attaching zero-initialized low-rank adapters to a frozen ViT or CLIP image encoder and training them offline to align corrupted hidden trajectories with those of cleaner inputs. The formulation supports both source-dependent adaptation using clean targets and source-free adaptation using corrupted/further-corrupted image pairs, with the latter requiring no clean source data. Once trained, the adapters remain fixed at inference, eliminating test-time gradients and per-sample optimization. The same formulation extends directly to CLIP zero-shot classification. • We introduce an online variant of Drift-TTA that adapts the strength of this learned trajectory correction at test time: Drift-TTA-online keeps the backbone and trained adapters frozen and updates only one scalar per adapter branch to control its correction strength. Each scalar scales the correction vector produced by its adapter and is optimized using prediction entropy on each unlabeled target batch. The same procedure applies to both source-dependent and source-free adapters. • We provide a probabilistic interpretation and theoretical bounds for hidden-trajectory alignment: We interpret the trajectory-alignment objective as regularized MAP estimation under a Gaussian observation model. We then derive a KL-based transfer bound and an explicit Gaussian form relating test-time residual error to offline residual error, residual dimensionality, and offline-to-test distribution shift. • We establish that hidden-trajectory alignment consistently improves corruption robustness and calibration across models: On CIFAR-100-C at severity 5, source-dependent Drift-TTA-online improves mean accuracy by 16.6 % 16.6\% and 13.0 % 13.0\% over the unadapted ViT-B/16 and CLIP ViT-B/16, respectively, while exceeding the strongest compared TTA baselines by 2.5 % 2.5\% and 6.2 % 6.2\% . It also improves calibration, reducing mean ECE relative to these baselines by 9.94 % 9.94\% for ViT and 9.69 % 9.69\% for CLIP.

sections.heading: 2  Background and Related Work
sections.text: This section introduces the test time adaptation setting, reviews existing methods, and summarizes Chain-of-Embedding ( Wang et al., 2025a ) , which motivates this work.

sections.heading: 2.1  Test Time Adaptation
sections.text: Test time adaptation modifies a pretrained model using unlabeled test samples during test time. The labels of the test samples are never available for adaptation, and many methods also assume that the data used to train the pretrained model are unavailable at test time ( Wang et al., 2021 ) . Let f ω f_{\omega} denote a model with pretrained parameters ω \omega , trained on source inputs x s x_{s} and labels y s y_{s} . At test time, the model receives inputs x t x_{t} without their labels y t y_{t} . Let α \alpha denote the variables adapted at test time, and let ℒ t \mathcal{L}_{t} be an unlabeled test time objective. Definition 2.1 (Test time adaptation) . Optimization-based test time adaptation estimates α ⋆ = arg ⁡ min α ​ ℒ t ​ ( f ω , α ​ ( x t ) ) , y ^ t = f ω , α ⋆ ​ ( x t ) , \alpha^{\star}=\arg\min_{\alpha}\mathcal{L}_{t}\bigl(f_{\omega,\alpha}(x_{t})\bigr),\qquad\hat{y}_{t}=f_{\omega,\alpha^{\star}}(x_{t}), (1) without using y t y_{t} . Adaptation is online when each test batch x t x_{t} is used as it arrives. Existing methods differ mainly in the objective ℒ t \mathcal{L}_{t} that guides adaptation, the variables α \alpha they adapt, and how they use the test inputs x t x_{t} . A common approach is to use the model predictions themselves to guide adaptation. Tent ( Wang et al., 2021 ) minimizes prediction entropy while updating the affine parameters of normalization layers. EATA ( Niu et al., 2022 ) builds on entropy minimization by selecting reliable test samples and regularizing important model parameters using Fisher information, while SAR ( Niu et al., 2023 ) combines entropy minimization with sample filtering and sharpness-aware optimization to improve stability. For continual test streams, CMF ( Lee and Chang, 2024 ) further filters the information used during adaptation to reduce forgetting. Other methods use related signals from the model output, learn how the update itself should be performed, or use auxiliary tasks during adaptation ( Choi et al., 2025 ; Deng et al., 2025 ; Alfarra et al., 2026 ) . Despite these differences, the model predictions remain the main signal used for adaptation. Other methods use information from the model representations themselves. FOA ( Niu et al., 2024 ) combines prediction entropy with feature statistics and adapts prompts and activations using derivative-free optimization. PEA ( Ma et al., 2026 ) instead uses feature statistics across intermediate layers to progressively align hidden representations without backpropagation. Related work also operates on latent features or their geometry ( Murphy et al., 2026 ; Bao et al., 2025a ; Lei et al., 2025 ; Cho et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2022 ; Wang et al., 2023 ) . These methods show that intermediate representations can also provide useful signals for adaptation. For vision-language models such as CLIP ( Radford et al., 2021 ) , TTA has also been extended to prompts, tokens, memories, and class representations ( Zhang et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025b ; Bao et al., 2025b ) . TPT ( Shu et al., 2022 ) adapts the text prompt for each test image using prediction entropy. TDA ( Karmanov et al., 2024 ) and DMN-ZS ( Zhang et al., 2024b ) instead accumulate information from test samples using feature caches or dynamic memories. BCA ( Zhou et al., 2025 ) adapts class embeddings together with their priors, while DPE ( Zhang et al., 2024a ) evolves visual and textual class prototypes using entropy and cross-modal alignment. More recently, BAT ( Maharana et al., 2025b ) adapts the LayerNorm parameters of both the vision and text encoders using entropy and alignment, while BITTA ( Sun et al., 2026 ) additionally uses high-entropy samples for unlearning. Other work also considers how adaptation is applied across layers or maintained over longer test streams ( Maharana et al., 2025a ; Vray et al., 2025 ) . These methods are commonly evaluated on the -C benchmarks ( Hendrycks and Dietterich, 2019 ) , including CIFAR-10-C, CIFAR-100-C, and ImageNet-C, which apply fifteen corruption families at five severity levels. Online, instance-level, episodic adaptation processes each sample as it arrives and resets before the next, making it more constrained than offline, batch-level, or continual settings. Drift-TTA-online supports this setting and can also operate on batches when multiple samples are available. Overall, existing TTA methods use a range of adaptation signals, including model outputs, feature statistics, memories, pseudo-labels, cross-modal alignment, and intermediate representations.

sections.heading: Chain-of-Embedding.
sections.text: Chain-of-Embedding (CoE) ( Wang et al., 2025a ) studies how hidden representations evolve across layers in large language models. It shows that geometric summaries of this sequence can separate correct from incorrect generations. We transfer this view from language model outcomes to vision models under corrupted inputs. Specifically, we compare clean and corrupted versions of the same input across network depth to study how corruption changes the learned representations.

sections.heading: Source-dependent training.
sections.text: Source-dependent training starts from a clean source image 𝐱 clean \mathbf{x}^{\mathrm{clean}} and corrupts it with a corruption operator 𝒞 \mathcal{C} , giving the student input 𝐱 = 𝒞 ⁡ ( 𝐱 clean ) \mathbf{x}=\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{x}^{\mathrm{clean}}) . The clean image serves as both the teacher view and the anchor, 𝐱 tgt = 𝐱 anc = 𝐱 clean \mathbf{x}^{\mathrm{tgt}}=\mathbf{x}^{\mathrm{anc}}=\mathbf{x}^{\mathrm{clean}} . The adapters therefore learn to move the corrupted trajectory back toward the hidden trajectory and decision of the clean forward pass.

sections.heading: Source-free training.
sections.text: When clean images are unavailable, source-free training starts from a corrupted image 𝐱 cur \mathbf{x}^{\mathrm{cur}} and corrupts it further, giving the student input 𝐱 = 𝐱 + = Worsen ⁡ ( 𝐱 cur ) \mathbf{x}=\mathbf{x}^{+}=\operatorname{Worsen}(\mathbf{x}^{\mathrm{cur}}) with the same corruption family at a higher effective severity. The current image then serves as both the cleaner teacher view and the anchor, 𝐱 tgt = 𝐱 anc = 𝐱 cur \mathbf{x}^{\mathrm{tgt}}=\mathbf{x}^{\mathrm{anc}}=\mathbf{x}^{\mathrm{cur}} , so no clean images or class labels are required. The adapters thus learn to move the trajectory of 𝐱 + \mathbf{x}^{+} back toward that of 𝐱 cur \mathbf{x}^{\mathrm{cur}} , although this target trajectory remains corrupted. At deployment, the learned correction is applied to the current corrupted input and partially reverses the same direction of displacement. For stochastic corruptions, the worsening operation preserves the underlying corruption realization whenever possible, since an independent draw can change the displacement direction and weaken the teacher correspondence.

sections.heading: 4  Experiments
sections.text: Drift-TTA is applied to both unimodal classifiers and CLIP-based classification models. In this section, we report comprehensive validation for our approach. The experimental setting is described in Section 4.1 . Main results are presented in Section 4.2 .

sections.heading: 4.1  Experimental Setup
sections.text: Datasets and models. We evaluate Drift-TTA on CIFAR-10-C, CIFAR-100-C, and ImageNet-C ( Hendrycks and Dietterich, 2019 ) , each containing 15 corruption types at five severity levels. For unimodal classification, ViT-Tiny is used on CIFAR-10-C, while ViT-B/16 is used on CIFAR-100-C and ImageNet-C. Each model is pretrained on the corresponding clean dataset. For CLIP-based classification, we use a pretrained CLIP ViT-B/16 model. Both source-dependent and source-free variants of Drift-TTA are evaluated. Training Protocol. Drift-TTA adds a lightweight LoRA adapter (rank 4, on all transformer blocks) to a frozen backbone. For each corruption family we train one adapter on the other 14 families (all five severities) and evaluate on the held-out family; Table 3 reports this leave-one-family-out accuracy. The adapter weights are trained offline and remain frozen at test time. Drift-TTA-online updates only their scalar gates using prediction entropy on the current unlabeled target batch. Source-dependent is trained for 4000 steps, while source-free adapters are trained for 2400 steps. A held-out validation split is used only to monitor convergence. For supervised ViT runs, the final checkpoint is reported. For CLIP, we select among epochs 1,3,5,7,9 using unsupervised validation loss; no target labels are used for model selection.. Evaluation. Each adapted model is compared with the corresponding model without adaptation on the same corrupted images. Source-dependent experiments use 2,000 2{,}000 CIFAR and 5,000 5{,}000 ImageNet images, while source-free experiments use 10,000 10{,}000 CIFAR and 50,000 50{,}000 ImageNet images. CLIP experiments use 10,000 10{,}000 CIFAR and 5,000 5{,}000 ImageNet images. We primarily report the change in accuracy relative to no adaptation, denoted by Δ \Delta pp. Recovery and changes in clean accuracy are also reported when applicable. All experiments use a single seed, with an expected run-to-run variation of approximately 0.3 % 0.3\% .

sections.heading: 5  Conclusion
sections.text: In this work, we studied hidden trajectories of neural networks for test-time adaptation under distribution shift. We observed that clean and corrupted trajectories become more separable as corruption severity increases, motivating Drift-TTA . Our approach uses low-rank adapters to correct trajectory drift while keeping the pretrained backbone frozen. Drift-TTA supports both source-dependent and source-free training, and can be used either as a fixed correction or with lightweight online adaptation using unlabeled test data. We also provided a probabilistic interpretation of trajectory alignment and theoretical bounds for offline generalization and source-free correction. Experiments on CIFAR-10-C, CIFAR-100-C, and ImageNet-C with supervised ViTs and CLIP demonstrate improved robustness to corruption, while reducing expected calibration error (ECE) relative to prior TTA baselines. Overall, these results highlight hidden trajectory alignment as an effective signal for test-time adaptation.

sections.heading: A.1  Adapter Implementation
sections.text: Each adapter is realized as a forward hook on a target linear layer, so no model code is modified. The hook computes the low-rank correction 𝑨 l ​ 𝑩 l ​ 𝒙 {\bm{A}}_{l}{\bm{B}}_{l}{\bm{x}} and adds it to the layer’s output, which already contains 𝑾 l ​ 𝒙 + 𝒃 l {\bm{W}}_{l}{\bm{x}}+{\bm{b}}_{l} . A single flag enables or disables all hooks at once, which makes the paired “adapters-on versus adapters-off” evaluation trivial. The up-projection 𝑨 l {\bm{A}}_{l} is zero-initialized and the down-projection 𝑩 l {\bm{B}}_{l} is drawn from 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , 10 − 3 ) \mathcal{N}(0,10^{-3}) , so the branch is an exact no-op at initialization; only 𝑨 l , 𝑩 l {\bm{A}}_{l},{\bm{B}}_{l} receive gradients. Each trained set of adapter factors is stored as a single checkpoint per variant. We reiterate that 𝑨 l ​ 𝑩 l {\bm{A}}_{l}{\bm{B}}_{l} is a learned side branch and not a factorization of 𝑾 l {\bm{W}}_{l} : no singular-value decomposition or low-rank approximation of the pretrained weights is ever computed. In the supervised ViT the adapted layers are the two MLP projections and the attention output projection of each block ( mlp.fc1 , mlp.fc2 , attn.proj ), excluding the fused qkv projection; in the CLIP image tower they are the two MLP projections of each residual attention block ( mlp.c_fc , mlp.c_proj ).

sections.heading: A.2  Training Details
sections.text: Adapters are trained with Adam at learning rate 10 − 3 10^{-3} and batch size 64 64 ( 32 32 on ImageNet). The source budget is 2,000 2{,}000 images for CIFAR and 3,000 3{,}000 for ImageNet (about three per class). The objective uses uniform trajectory weights w l = 1 w_{l}{=}1 over the aligned blocks, a decision weight λ dec = 1.0 \lambda_{\mathrm{dec}}{=}1.0 , a control weight λ ctrl = 10 − 3 \lambda_{\mathrm{ctrl}}{=}10^{-3} , and a quietness weight λ quiet = 0.05 \lambda_{\mathrm{quiet}}{=}0.05 . Supervised runs use a fixed number of epochs (five for CIFAR, two for ImageNet); the CLIP runs train to E max = 9 E_{\max}=9 and select the checkpoint on the grid { 1 , 3 , 5 , 7 , 9 } \{1,3,5,7,9\} by label-free validation loss.

sections.heading: Appendix D Single-Model Generalization to Unseen Corruption Families
sections.text: The per-corruption tables above follow the leave-one-family-out (LOFO) protocol, in which a separate Drift-TTA adapter is trained for each held-out corruption; a full fifteen-family table therefore aggregates fifteen independently trained adapters. Prior test-time adaptation methods instead deploy a single model that must cope with any corruption, so this asymmetry could be raised against a direct comparison. To remove it, we train one Drift-TTA adapter on the fifteen standard corruption families and evaluate it, with no further training, on the four validation corruptions distributed with the -C benchmarks that are disjoint from the training families: speckle noise , Gaussian blur , spatter , and saturate . This is a strict, single-model, apples-to-apples setting: exactly as for the baselines, one model adapts to all four unseen corruptions, in both its offline form (the frozen adapter) and its online form (the adapter with entropy-based gate calibration), under source-dependent (SD) and source-free (SF) training. Tables 7 – 9 report accuracy at severity 5 on ImageNet-C, CIFAR-10-C, and CIFAR-100-C, against the strongest single-model baseline for each backbone (PEA for ViT, BITTA for CLIP). Across all three benchmarks and both backbones, Drift-TTA improves over the unadapted model and over the baseline, showing that the trajectory-repair prior transfers to corruption families never seen during training. sections.heading: Appendix E Calibration (Expected Calibration Error)
sections.text: Beyond accuracy, we report expected calibration error (ECE, %, ↓ \downarrow ) at severity 5 for all three benchmarks and both backbones. For each setting we compare the unadapted model (No-TTA) and the strongest prior test-time-adaptation baseline (PEA for the unimodal ViT, BITTA for CLIP) against Drift-TTA (the frozen repair adapter) and Drift-TTA-online (the same adapter with its per-branch gates tuned online by entropy minimization), under both source-dependent (SD) and source-free (SF) training. ECE uses 15 equal-width bins over the top-label confidence, on the same corrupted evaluation sets and configurations used for the accuracy tables. The best SD and SF variants reduce mean ECE relative to PEA and BITTA across all model–dataset settings. Table 4 summarizes these results in the main text. Tables 10 – 12 give the full per-corruption breakdown.

sections.heading: Appendix F Hidden-Trajectory Drift under Corruption
sections.text: This section explains how each panel of Figure 4 is constructed and how it should be interpreted. We first define the trajectory quantities shown in the figure, then examine whether the association between trajectory drift and prediction error remains after controlling for corruption severity. Figure 5 provides the corresponding analysis on ImageNet-C.

sections.heading: Experimental setup.
sections.text: We evaluate a frozen ViT-B/16 without test-time adaptation. CIFAR-100-C contains N = 10,000 N{=}10{,}000 images per corruption condition, while ImageNet-C contains N = 50,000 N{=}50{,}000 . Each corrupted image is paired with its clean counterpart, and both are processed by the same frozen model. Consequently, trajectory drift and prediction error are measured on the same images. Panels (a) and (e) use one representative corruption family—Gaussian noise for CIFAR-100-C and fog for ImageNet-C—while panels (b) – (d) summarize all fifteen corruption families. sections.text: Panel (e) provides an image-level view of trajectory geometry. Each image is represented by the magnitude and angle features defined in Section 3 . sections.heading: Controlling for corruption severity.
sections.text: Across the 75 75 CIFAR-100-C conditions, relative trajectory drift and top-1 error have Pearson correlation r = 0.73 r{=}0.73 and Spearman correlation ρ s = 0.78 \rho_{s}{=}0.78 . Both quantities generally increase with corruption severity, so we additionally test whether the association remains when severity is held fixed. Within each severity level, Pearson correlation remains positive and ranges from 0.59 0.59 to 0.71 0.71 across the fifteen corruption families. After subtracting the corresponding severity-level mean from both drift and error, their residual Pearson correlation is r = 0.63 r{=}0.63 . The corresponding partial Spearman correlation is ρ s = 0.67 \rho_{s}{=}0.67 . The five severity levels of a corruption family are related and should not be treated as independent observations. We therefore resample complete corruption-family profiles, retaining all five severities whenever a family is selected. This family-cluster bootstrap gives a 95 % 95\% confidence interval of [ 0.39 , 0.83 ] [0.39,0.83] for the severity-controlled Pearson correlation. A complementary permutation test that reassigns complete five-severity drift profiles across corruption families gives p < 0.01 p{<}0.01 . Thus, the observed association is not explained only by the shared increase of drift and error with corruption severity.

sections.text: To visualize how adaptation changes the class structure of the representations used for classification, we project these features to two dimensions using UMAP and t-SNE and color each point by its true class. All panels use the complete CIFAR-10-C test set of 10,000 10{,}000 images at severity 5 under the leave-one-family-out protocol. We show six corruption families spanning noise, blur, weather, and digital corruptions. Each panel is projected independently, so absolute positions and axis directions should not be compared across panels. The intended comparison is the compactness and separation of the class distributions within each panel. UMAP and t-SNE provide complementary views and show the same qualitative progression: relative to No Adaptation, the fixed Drift-TTA adapters generally produce more compact and better-separated class distributions, while online gate adaptation further improves this structure. Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.24220v1 [cs.LG] 16 Oct 2026 Hidden Trajectories Don’t Lie: Correcting Corruption Drift for Test-Time Adaptation Amirhossein Sabour 1,2,* Amir Khasahmadi 1 Mengliu Zhao 1, † \dagger 1 Autodesk Research 2 McMaster University {amirhossein.sabour,amir.khasahmadi,mengliu.zhao}@autodesk.com 1 1 footnotetext: This study was conducted during the author’s internship at Autodesk Research. 2 2 footnotetext: Corresponding author: mengliu.zhao@autodesk.com Abstract Test-time adaptation (TTA) adapts pretrained models to distribution shifts encountered during deployment. However, most existing methods rely primarily on the weight representations of the final layer or signals derived from the model’s output probability distribution. In this work, we study hidden trajectories : the ordered sequence of intermediate representations produced across a deep neural network. We observe that clean and corrupted trajectories become more separable as corruption severity increases. Based on this observation, we introduce Drift-TTA , which adds zero-initialized low-rank adapters to a frozen backbone and trains them to align corrupted hidden trajectories with those from cleaner inputs. The proposed approach supports two variants: a source-dependent version trained with clean targets, and a source-free setting that learns from corrupted images at different severities. Building on these two variants, we further develop an online TTA approach that freezes the backbone and adapters while updating a scalar gate to control adaptation strength. We further cast trajectory alignment as MAP inference under a Gaussian observation model and derive a KL-based transfer bound characterizing test-time trajectory misalignment in terms of offline residual error, residual dimensionality, and distribution shift between offline and test corruptions. We evaluate Drift-TTA on CIFAR-10-C, CIFAR-100-C, and ImageNet-C using supervised ViTs and CLIP models. On CIFAR-100-C at severity 5, our source-free online approach improves accuracy over no TTA by 13.3 percentage points with ViT-B/16 and 11.6 percentage points with CLIP ViT-B/16, reaching 74.9% and 47.4%, respectively. Under the same setting, prior TTA baselines yield ECEs of 18.00% for ViT and 14.70% for CLIP, while our approach reduces them to 9.53% and 5.77%, respectively. These results demonstrate that hidden trajectory alignment provides an effective signal for both offline correction and lightweight online test-time adaptation. 1 Introduction Test time adaptation (TTA) adapts a pretrained model to unlabeled test data during deployment, when corruptions such as sensor noise, weather, blur, and compression artifacts shift inputs away from the clean source distribution ( Hendrycks and Dietterich, 2019 ) . Many recent methods guide adaptation using prediction-derived objectives, learned update mechanisms, or auxiliary self-supervised signals ( Liang et al., 2025 ; Xiao and Snoek, 2024 ) . Some minimize entropy or use related confidence and energy objectives to update a small set of model parameters, including the affine parameters of batch normalization layers ( Wang et al., 2021 ; Choi et al., 2025 ) , while others adapt representations or features directly ( Murphy et al., 2026 ; Cho et al., 2025 ) . These studies demonstrate the potential of TTA to recover much of the accuracy lost on standard corruption benchmarks, often with modest computation and without source labels during test time. Entropy minimization is the primary approach in TTA, with several methods extending it through related confidence- and energy-based objectives ( Deng et al., 2025 ; Lei et al., 2025 ) . However, these objectives encourage the model to produce more confident predictions, but do not directly optimize whether those predictions are correct. As a result, an incorrect prediction can become more confident without necessarily being corrected. Furthermore, intermediate features remain comparatively underexplored in TTA, both in how they change as corruption severity increases and in whether they can provide a complementary signal for adaptation. To examine this, we look beyond the final output or a single representation and follow how features evolve through the network. Chain-of-Embedding ( Wang et al., 2025a ) provides a framework for this by representing a forward pass as a trajectory of hidden states whose geometry can differ across outcomes. We extend this view to vision under corruption and examine whether clean and corrupted inputs trace distinguishable trajectories through a ViT or CLIP image tower. Across all models we test, features derived from the hidden trajectory separate clean and corrupted inputs more clearly as corruption severity increases. This observation motivates Drift-TTA , which adds zero-initialized low-rank adapters ( Hu et al., 2022 ) to a frozen backbone and trains them so that corrupted inputs produce hidden trajectories closer to those of their clean counterparts. Figure 1 summarizes this intuition. Corruption progressively displaces the hidden trajectory as severity increases, while Drift-TTA learns a correction in the opposite direction and shifts the resulting trajectory features back toward the clean distribution. Figure 1: Corruption progressively shifts hidden trajectories, while Drift-TTA moves them back toward clean. (a) Schematic of severity-dependent trajectory drift and the correction learned by Drift-TTA. (b) Distributions of the trajectory magnitude and angle features for clean and corrupted inputs at severities 1–5, before and after applying Drift-TTA. Each column compares clean inputs with one corruption severity. Without adaptation, the corrupted distributions move farther from clean as severity increases. With Drift-TTA, they shift back toward the clean distribution. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • We introduce hidden trajectories as a vision-domain extension of the chain-of-embeddings framework previously studied in large language models: A hidden trajectory captures the ordered sequence of mean-pooled representations across backbone layers, and we show that trajectory-derived features increasingly separate clean from corrupted inputs as corruption severity grows across all tested vision models. • We introduce hidden-trajectory alignment as a deployment-efficient mechanism for corruption correction: Drift-TTA instantiates this idea by attaching zero-initialized low-rank adapters to a frozen ViT or CLIP image encoder and training them offline to align corrupted hidden trajectories with those of cleaner inputs. The formulation supports both source-dependent adaptation using clean targets and source-free adaptation using corrupted/further-corrupted image pairs, with the latter requiring no clean source data. Once trained, the adapters remain fixed at inference, eliminating test-time gradients and per-sample optimization. The same formulation extends directly to CLIP zero-shot classification. • We introduce an online variant of Drift-TTA that adapts the strength of this learned trajectory correction at test time: Drift-TTA-online keeps the backbone and trained adapters frozen and updates only one scalar per adapter branch to control its correction strength. Each scalar scales the correction vector produced by its adapter and is optimized using prediction entropy on each unlabeled target batch. The same procedure applies to both source-dependent and source-free adapters. • We provide a probabilistic interpretation and theoretical bounds for hidden-trajectory alignment: We interpret the trajectory-alignment objective as regularized MAP estimation under a Gaussian observation model. We then derive a KL-based transfer bound and an explicit Gaussian form relating test-time residual error to offline residual error, residual dimensionality, and offline-to-test distribution shift. • We establish that hidden-trajectory alignment consistently improves corruption robustness and calibration across models: On CIFAR-100-C at severity 5, source-dependent Drift-TTA-online improves mean accuracy by 16.6 % 16.6\% and 13.0 % 13.0\% over the unadapted ViT-B/16 and CLIP ViT-B/16, respectively, while exceeding the strongest compared TTA baselines by 2.5 % 2.5\% and 6.2 % 6.2\% . It also improves calibration, reducing mean ECE relative to these baselines by 9.94 % 9.94\% for ViT and 9.69 % 9.69\% for CLIP. 2 Background and Related Work This section introduces the test time adaptation setting, reviews existing methods, and summarizes Chain-of-Embedding ( Wang et al., 2025a ) , which motivates this work. 2.1 Test Time Adaptation Test time adaptation modifies a pretrained model using unlabeled test samples during test time. A common approach is to use the model predictions themselves to guide adaptation. Tent ( Wang et al., 2021 ) minimizes prediction entropy while updating the affine parameters of normalization layers. EATA ( Niu et al., 2022 ) builds on entropy minimization by selecting reliable test samples and regularizing important model parameters using Fisher information, while SAR ( Niu et al., 2023 ) combines entropy minimization with sample filtering and sharpness-aware optimization to improve stability. For continual test streams, CMF ( Lee and Chang, 2024 ) further filters the information used during adaptation to reduce forgetting. Other methods use related signals from the model output, learn how the update itself should be performed, or use auxiliary tasks during adaptation ( Choi et al., 2025 ; Deng et al., 2025 ; Alfarra et al., 2026 ) . Despite these differences, the model predictions remain the main signal used for adaptation. Other methods use information from the model representations themselves. FOA ( Niu et al., 2024 ) combines prediction entropy with feature statistics and adapts prompts and activations using derivative-free optimization. PEA ( Ma et al., 2026 ) instead uses feature statistics across intermediate layers to progressively align hidden representations without backpropagation. Related work also operates on latent features or their geometry ( Murphy et al., 2026 ; Bao et al., 2025a ; Lei et al., 2025 ; Cho et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2022 ; Wang et al., 2023 ) . These methods show that intermediate representations can also provide useful signals for adaptation. For vision-language models such as CLIP ( Radford et al., 2021 ) , TTA has also been extended to prompts, tokens, memories, and class representations ( Zhang et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025b ; Bao et al., 2025b ) . TPT ( Shu et al., 2022 ) adapts the text prompt for each test image using prediction entropy. TDA ( Karmanov et al., 2024 ) and DMN-ZS ( Zhang et al., 2024b ) instead accumulate information from test samples using feature caches or dynamic memories. BCA ( Zhou et al., 2025 ) adapts class embeddings together with their priors, while DPE ( Zhang et al., 2024a ) evolves visual and textual class prototypes using entropy and cross-modal alignment. More recently, BAT ( Maharana et al., 2025b ) adapts the LayerNorm parameters of both the vision and text encoders using entropy and alignment, while BITTA ( Sun et al., 2026 ) additionally uses high-entropy samples for unlearning. Other work also considers how adaptation is applied across layers or maintained over longer test streams ( Maharana et al., 2025a ; Vray et al., 2025 ) . We evaluate Drift-TTA on CIFAR-10-C, CIFAR-100-C, and ImageNet-C ( Hendrycks and Dietterich, 2019 ) , each containing 15 corruption types at five severity levels. For CLIP-based classification, we use a pretrained CLIP ViT-B/16 model. Both source-dependent and source-free variants of Drift-TTA are evaluated. Training Protocol. Drift-TTA adds a lightweight LoRA adapter (rank 4, on all transformer blocks) to a frozen backbone. For each corruption family we train one adapter on the other 14 families (all five severities) and evaluate on the held-out family; Table 3 reports this leave-one-family-out accuracy. The adapter weights are trained offline and remain frozen at test time. Drift-TTA-online updates only their scalar gates using prediction entropy on the current unlabeled target batch. Source-dependent is trained for 4000 steps, while source-free adapters are trained for 2400 steps. A held-out validation split is used only to monitor convergence. For supervised ViT runs, the final checkpoint is reported. For CLIP, we select among epochs 1,3,5,7,9 using unsupervised validation loss; no target labels are used for model selection.. Evaluation. Each adapted model is compared with the corresponding model without adaptation on the same corrupted images. Source-dependent experiments use 2,000 2{,}000 CIFAR and 5,000 5{,}000 ImageNet images, while source-free experiments use 10,000 10{,}000 CIFAR and 50,000 50{,}000 ImageNet images. CLIP experiments use 10,000 10{,}000 CIFAR and 5,000 5{,}000 ImageNet images. We primarily report the change in accuracy relative to no adaptation, denoted by Δ \Delta pp. Recovery and changes in clean accuracy are also reported when applicable.
